name: uname
summary: Print kernel name, release and machine architecture; see also /etc/os-release for the distribution.
compat: /etc/os-release exists on systemd-era distributions and most Yocto/Buildroot images; very old or custom systems may lack it.

examples.title: Kernel release
examples.explain: Prints e.g. 6.8.0-45-generic. Out-of-tree kernel modules must be built against headers for exactly this release (often found under /lib/modules/$(uname -r)/build).

examples.title: Machine architecture
examples.explain: x86_64 for a typical PC, aarch64 or armv7l on many boards. Binaries must be compiled for this architecture.

examples.title: Everything in one line
examples.explain: Kernel name, host name, release, build version and architecture. Good to paste into bug reports.

examples.title: Which distribution and version is this?
examples.explain: NAME, VERSION_ID and ID tell you the distribution (e.g. ubuntu, debian, fedora, poky for Yocto), which decides the package manager to use.

name: free
compat: The same data is in /proc/meminfo, which exists on every Linux system including minimal embedded ones.

examples.title: Memory in human-readable units
examples.explain: Look at the 'available' column, not 'free'. Linux uses idle RAM as disk cache (buff/cache) and gives it back when programs need it, so low 'free' is normal.

examples.title: Raw kernel memory statistics
examples.explain: MemTotal, MemFree and MemAvailable in kB, straight from the kernel. Works where free is not installed.

name: uptime
summary: How long the system has been running and its load average; with nproc, judge whether it is overloaded.
compat: Linux load average counts tasks running or waiting for CPU and tasks in uninterruptible I/O wait.

examples.title: Uptime and load average
examples.explain: The three numbers are 1, 5 and 15 minute load averages. Compare them with the number of CPUs: on 4 CPUs, a load of 4 means fully busy.

examples.title: Number of CPUs available
examples.explain: Commonly used for parallel builds: make -j"$(nproc)".

name: df
summary: Show free and used space on mounted file systems.

examples.title: All file systems, human-readable
examples.explain: Use% near 100% on / or /home causes 'No space left on device'. tmpfs entries live in RAM.

examples.title: Which file system holds this directory?
examples.explain: Shows only the file system containing the current directory, e.g. before a large Yocto build.

examples.title: Check inode usage
examples.explain: A disk can be 'full' because it ran out of inodes (too many small files) while df -h still shows free space.
options: Show inode usage instead of blocks

name: du
summary: Measure how much disk space directories and files use.
compat: --max-depth is GNU; BusyBox uses -d 1 (GNU also accepts -d).

examples.title: Total size of a directory
examples.explain: -s gives one summary line instead of listing every subdirectory.

examples.title: Size of each subdirectory, biggest last
examples.explain: Descend one level and sort by size. Repeat inside the biggest entry to drill down to what is using space.

name: lsblk
summary: List block devices (disks, SD cards, USB sticks, partitions) as a tree.
compat: Device names: sdX = SATA/USB disks, nvme0n1 = NVMe, mmcblk0 = SD/eMMC. Names can change between boots and when devices are plugged in.

examples.title: Show all disks and partitions
examples.explain: TYPE disk is a whole device, part a partition. RM 1 marks removable media. Run it before and after inserting an SD card to see which name appears.

examples.title: Include file system types and labels
examples.explain: Shows FSTYPE (ext4, vfat...), LABEL, UUID and where each is mounted.

examples.title: Choose columns, including the device model
examples.explain: MODEL and SIZE help you be sure which device is the SD card reader before writing an image.

name: lscpu
summary: Show CPU architecture, model, core count, byte order and cache sizes.
compat: On systems without lscpu, read /proc/cpuinfo; its format differs between x86 and ARM.

examples.title: CPU summary
examples.explain: Check Architecture, Byte Order (little endian on almost all ARM and x86 Linux systems), CPU(s) and Model name.

examples.title: Raw per-CPU information from the kernel
examples.explain: On ARM boards this often includes Hardware/Revision lines identifying the SoC.

name: mount
summary: Attach (mount) and detach (umount) file systems; findmnt shows what is mounted where.
compat: Desktop environments usually auto-mount removable media under /media or /run/media. 'target is busy' on umount means a process (or a shell sitting in that directory) still uses it; check with lsof.

examples.title: Which mount contains this directory?
examples.explain: Shows the source device, file system type and mount options (e.g. ro = read-only).
options: Find the mount containing this path

examples.title: Mount a partition on an empty directory
examples.explain: <partition> is a device such as /dev/sdb1 (find it with lsblk); <mount-point> is an existing empty directory. The file system type is usually detected automatically.
examples.warning: Mounting on a non-empty directory hides its contents until unmounted. Make sure you picked the right partition with lsblk -f.
options: Existing directory to attach it to

examples.title: Unmount before removing the card
examples.explain: Flushes pending writes and detaches the file system. Always unmount before pulling an SD card or USB stick, or data may be lost.
examples.warning: Programs using files on that mount lose access. Do not use lazy/force options unless you understand the consequences.

name: lsusb
summary: List USB devices with their vendor and product IDs.
compat: Inside WSL, containers or VMs, USB devices are only visible if passed through to that environment.

examples.title: List connected USB devices
examples.explain: Each line shows bus, device number and ID vendor:product (e.g. 0403:6001 is a common FTDI serial adapter). If your device is missing, it is a cable, power or hardware problem rather than a driver one.

examples.title: Tree view with the driver bound to each interface
examples.explain: Driver=... shows which kernel driver claimed each interface; Driver=[none] means no driver matched.

examples.title: Detailed descriptors for one device
examples.explain: Prints the full descriptors (interfaces, endpoints) that a USB driver matches against. Some fields need root to read and show as warnings otherwise.

name: lspci
summary: List PCI/PCIe devices and the kernel driver that is using each one.
compat: Many ARM boards have no PCI bus at all; their devices are described by the device tree instead.

examples.title: List PCI devices
examples.explain: Each line: bus address, device class (e.g. Ethernet controller) and name.

examples.title: Show which driver handles each device
examples.explain: 'Kernel driver in use' is the bound driver; 'Kernel modules' lists drivers that could handle it. A device with no driver in use explains a missing network or Wi-Fi interface.

examples.title: Show numeric vendor and device IDs
examples.explain: IDs like [8086:15b8] are what a driver's PCI ID table matches.
options: Show both names and numeric IDs

name: dd
summary: Copy raw bytes between files and devices; used to create test files and to write disk images to SD cards.
compat: status=progress and conv=fsync are GNU options; BusyBox dd supports conv=fsync but not status=progress. Tools such as bmaptool (for Yocto .wic images) are faster and add checks.

examples.title: Create a 10 MiB test file of zeros
examples.explain: if = input file, of = output file, bs = block size, count = number of blocks. Prints records in/out and the transfer rate when finished.
examples.warning: of= is overwritten without asking. Use a new file name.

examples.title: Identify the SD card before writing anything
examples.explain: Inspect-first: note the device list, insert the card, run it again. The new disk (e.g. sdb or mmcblk0) with the size of your card is the target. Unmount its partitions before writing.

examples.title: Write an image to an SD card
examples.cmd: sudo dd if=<image-file> of=/dev/<device> bs=4M status=progress conv=fsync
examples.explain: <device> is the whole disk (sdb, mmcblk0), not a partition (sdb1). conv=fsync makes sure data reaches the card before dd exits.
examples.warning: This overwrites the ENTIRE target device with no confirmation. Choosing the wrong device (for example your system disk) destroys it. Triple-check <device> with lsblk, and unplug other external drives.
options: Flush to the device before exiting
